articles.title: Data splits and leakage
articles.concept: Leakage lets information unavailable at prediction time influence training or evaluation. Duplicate document revisions, future labels and transformations fitted on all data can produce optimistic results. The evaluation partition must represent the deployment boundary rather than an arbitrary set of rows.
articles.mechanism: Choose the independence unit before splitting: users, document families or time periods may matter more than rows. Fit learned preprocessing only on training data, freeze final evaluation data and audit both exact duplicates and related examples across partitions.
articles.boundary: A clean split reduces optimistic bias but does not remove annotation errors, domain shift or a poorly defined target.
articles.example: A synthetic handbook dataset groups all revisions of the same document before splitting its question rows.
articles.application: Use entity-aware or chronological validation for assistants operating on related support histories or evolving document collections.

articles.title: Neurons, perceptrons and MLPs
articles.concept: A neuron combines a weighted sum, a bias and usually an activation. A perceptron expresses a linear boundary; an MLP composes layers to learn intermediate representations. These numerical functions do not imply human-like understanding or explainability by themselves.
articles.mechanism: Write the input, weight and bias shapes before a forward pass. Each layer maps feature vectors to another representation. Without nonlinear activations, a stack of affine transformations remains one affine transformation, even when the implementation contains many named layers.
articles.boundary: Extra width and depth increase capacity and cost. First check splits, labels and preprocessing; overfitting is not solved by making the network larger.
articles.example: A toy two-feature network computes a dense layer and clips negative pre-activations with ReLU.
articles.application: Benchmark a small MLP on structured numerical features before introducing a transformer into an unrelated prediction task.

articles.title: Activation functions and saturation
articles.concept: Activations introduce nonlinearity into a neural network. Sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and GELU differ in range and gradient behavior. Their effects depend on the architecture, objective and input distribution; naming an activation does not establish a universal accuracy or performance advantage.
articles.mechanism: Inspect both values and derivatives over actual pre-activation ranges. Sigmoid saturates at extreme magnitudes, reducing its derivative. ReLU zeros negative values and can create persistently inactive units. Numerical stability, initialization and feature scaling all influence the resulting learning signal.
articles.boundary: ReLU does not guarantee immunity to vanishing gradients, and a saturated probability is not automatically calibrated confidence.
articles.example: A stable sigmoid uses different equivalent expressions on positive and negative inputs, avoiding exp overflow.
articles.application: Inspect activation and gradient distributions when training stalls before changing the network width or learning objective.

articles.title: Gradients and backpropagation
articles.concept: Backpropagation computes loss derivatives through a computation graph using the chain rule. An optimizer uses those derivatives and its own state to update parameters. Automatic differentiation does not select a valid objective, fix data leakage or prove a model will generalize.
articles.mechanism: Run the forward computation, form a scalar loss, apply the intended accumulation policy, differentiate and update. Monitor finite values and shapes. Check a hand-derived scalar gradient with central finite differences, recognizing that this diagnostic depends on step size and floating-point precision.
articles.boundary: Gradient accumulation can be intentional. Detaching a tensor or crossing a nondifferentiable boundary can remove a required learning path.
articles.example: For prediction w*x and squared error, compare the analytic derivative with losses evaluated at small positive and negative weight perturbations.
articles.application: Use gradient checks for custom objectives and finite-value instrumentation when a training run stops updating or becomes unstable.

def loss(w,x,y):return (w*x-y)**2

articles.title: NLP, tokens and tokenization
articles.concept: Tokenizers encode text into model-specific discrete units. A token is not necessarily a word, character or fixed byte count. Subword boundaries vary with vocabulary, script, punctuation and tokenizer version. The tokenizer is part of the model contract, not an interchangeable display utility.
articles.mechanism: Count the exact serialized prompt, including role delimiters and special tokens, with a compatible tokenizer. Reserve output capacity and preserve offsets when normalizing or segmenting documents. Character or byte heuristics can illustrate encoding behavior but cannot guarantee an LLM token budget.
articles.boundary: Changing token IDs changes their learned embedding meanings. Multilingual inputs can violate English-derived token heuristics even when their character count seems small.
articles.example: A synthetic accented string illustrates different Python character and UTF-8 byte counts; neither value is labeled as an actual LLM token count.
articles.application: Budget multilingual prompts and maintain traceable document offsets for extraction, retrieval and source citations.

articles.title: Embeddings and vector representations
articles.concept: Embeddings represent items as numeric vectors learned for a task. Similarity can propose retrieval candidates, but it does not certify truth, permission or equivalence. Meaningful scores depend on model compatibility, preprocessing, normalization and the chosen distance function.
articles.mechanism: Encode documents and queries in compatible spaces, validate dimensions and evaluate relevance on labeled examples. Cosine divides the dot product by norms, so zero vectors require a policy. Keep source versions and access metadata beside vectors rather than relying on geometry to encode permissions.
articles.boundary: Mixing old document embeddings with a new query model can return plausible-looking numbers with meaningless rankings. Index migrations need evaluation and rollback.
articles.example: A two-dimensional toy search compares identical, orthogonal and zero vectors using an explicit cosine implementation.
articles.application: Retrieve candidate evidence semantically, then enforce authorization, freshness and support checks before generating text.
articles.code:
import math
def cosine(a,b):
    if len(a)!=len(b):raise ValueError('dimensions')
    denominator=math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in a)*sum(y*y for y in b))
    return sum(x*y for x,y in zip(a,b))/denominator if denominator else 0.0
assert cosine([0,0],[1,2])==0
assert cosine([1,0],[0,1])==0
print(round(cosine([1,1],[1,1]),3))

articles.title: Probability and next-token prediction
articles.concept: An autoregressive language model predicts a distribution over the next token given context. Training loss and the later decoding policy are distinct. A likely token continuation can be fluent while its resulting claim remains unsupported by the permitted evidence.
articles.mechanism: Normalize logits with a stable softmax by subtracting their maximum before exponentiation. Compare observed targets with the distribution using a suitable loss. Distinguish changes to the model from changes to sampling, and assess final task outcomes in addition to held-out token prediction.
articles.boundary: Lower perplexity alone does not prove a factual assistant is safer or more useful. Token likelihood is not a direct confidence estimate for a real-world assertion.
articles.example: A synthetic vocabulary demonstrates stable normalization for large logits and invariance under a common additive shift.
articles.application: Use probability calculations to reason about generation while evaluating evidence support and user-task success separately.
articles.code:
import math
def softmax(xs):
    if not xs or not all(math.isfinite(x) for x in xs):raise ValueError('logits')
    values=[math.exp(x-max(xs)) for x in xs]
    return [x/sum(values) for x in values]
a=softmax([1000,1001,1002])
assert abs(sum(a)-1)<1e-12
assert all(abs(x-y)<1e-12 for x,y in zip(a,softmax([0,1,2])))
print([round(x,4) for x in a])

articles.title: GPT-style models, hallucinations and limits
articles.concept: GPT-style generation can produce unsupported or incorrect content that remains persuasive. Grounding, validation and abstention reduce particular failure modes but do not guarantee universal correctness. A citation must correspond to accessible evidence that actually supports the relevant claim.
articles.mechanism: Separate source availability, retrieval relevance, evidence coverage and answer faithfulness. Test missing, stale and conflicting evidence. Validate source IDs deterministically and evaluate semantic support separately; a valid-looking reference can still be attached to an unsupported assertion.
articles.boundary: A refusal policy can fail too. Measure unnecessary refusals alongside unsupported answers instead of declaring a system fully truthful after a few successful examples.
articles.example: A synthetic policy answer is checked against an allowed document-ID set. This identity check is explicitly not a proof of semantic entailment.
articles.application: Offer evidence-grounded assistance with a clear escalation or abstention path for missing and contradictory information.
